motion: January 6 was an existential threat to American democracy.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: Your resilience point mistakes survival for safety. A bridge can remain standing after an attack and still reveal a fatal weakness; January sixth exposed that weakness at the transfer of power, which supports the motion.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. Tonight's motion is whether January sixth was an existential threat to American democracy. Joanna supports it, and Ron opposes it. Each opening and closing lasts thirty seconds; crossfire lasts two and a half minutes, and I will give a ten-second cue. Address each other directly, keep answers brief, and let the other speaker finish before responding.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: January sixth put the peaceful transfer of power under direct attack. A crowd tried to halt a lawful result while officials faced pressure to abandon their duty. How can Ron call that merely a disturbance when democracy depends on accepting a loss? The danger was not only what happened that day; it was the permission it offered for future refusal.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: You have ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: That permission matters because a system can survive one shock yet be weakened when force becomes a usable political tool. That is why this was existential. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you very much indeed. All right. Could I please ask Ron to speak against the motion, please.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Joanna is right that force and pressure were wrong, but wrong does not mean existential. The system resisted, officials completed their work, and the lawful result stood. A democracy facing a serious attack and preserving its core rules has shown resilience, not near extinction. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That concludes round one. Now we move on to round two and in round two the debaters have a conversation, address one another directly. It runs two and a half minutes, starting the moment I stop. Go.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I do not call it merely a disturbance; I call it a grave but contained assault. The lawful transfer happened anyway, so Joanna must show that danger alone made democracy's survival genuinely uncertain.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Ron, a system is endangered whenever people treat a lawful result as optional. I believe every attack on a lawful transfer of power always threatens democracy, because it tells future losers that force may replace consent.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your weakest word is always. A threat is not automatically existential, and your rule erases the difference between an attack a democracy defeats and one that actually destroys its capacity to govern.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I say this attack does not threaten democracy. It threatened the peaceful transfer of power, and that makes it an existential threat to American democracy.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: But you can't have it both ways, you can't every attack on a lawful transfer of power always threatens democracy on one hand and then this attack does not threaten democracy the next.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: I use threat in two senses: the event may fail to end democracy, yet its challenge to lawful transfer can menace democracy's future. Both statements separate immediate collapse from existential danger, so I remain for the motion.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: The larger issue is whether emergency security rules should give officials wider power to restrict gatherings before they turn violent. Those powers can burden peaceful citizens, invite selective enforcement, and deserve strict limits in any future security policy.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Okay, I'm not sure that that's getting to january sixth was an existential threat to american democracy, which I think is a little bit more on point.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: On the motion, January sixth was a severe attack but not an existential threat to American democracy. Its institutions processed the challenge, rejected coercion, and completed the lawful transfer without surrendering their authority.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When officials had to pause their work while a crowd sought to stop certification, the country saw force interrupt a constitutional duty. That example proves the danger was aimed at democracy's central mechanism, not a side issue.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your example proves disruption, not extinction. A pause is precisely what institutions can recover from, and the work resumed under the same rules, showing that the central mechanism endured rather than collapsed.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Ron, if force can be used to pressure officials whenever a side loses, what prevents the next losing side from trying again with greater coordination? Please answer how democracy remains safe under that lesson.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Just, just about ten seconds left.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I grant that repetition would be dangerous and demands accountability. But a warning about what might happen later-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Time's up. We are about to hear brief closing remarks from each debater in turn. On to round three, closing statements. First summarizing her position in support of the motion january sixth was an existential threat to american democracy, Joanna.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: January sixth was not simply angry speech or disorder around a political event. It was an effort to stop a lawful transfer by pressure and force. Democracy depends on losers accepting rules even when they hate the outcome. Once force is offered as an alternative, the system's future is placed in danger.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Ron points to the result, but a democracy is not secure merely because it survived one test. The event showed how quickly a lawful outcome could be challenged, and future actors-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Joanna, that's your time. Thank you. And now, Ron.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Deciding this motion turns on the meaning of existential. January sixth was dangerous, wrongful, and worthy of serious condemnation, but democracy's core process continued and the lawful result prevailed. Calling every grave challenge existential confuses resilience with collapse, so the motion is false. That's all, thank you.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Joanna and Ron, for a direct debate on a difficult question, and thank you for listening.
